extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students learning proofs and basic set-theoretic foundations of functions
extracted.subtask_description: Introductory treatment of functions as special relations between sets: precise definitions (function, domain, codomain, range), equality of functions, injective/surjective/bijective, proof techniques, composition, pigeonhole principle, and inverse relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function (set-theoretic) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f from A to B (f : A → B) is a relation f ⊆ A × B such that for each a ∈ A the relation f contains exactly one ordered pair of the form (a,b). The statement (a,b) ∈ f is abbreviated f(a) = b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formalizes the vertical-line-test idea: for each input a there is exactly one output. The text emphasizes thinking of a function as a concrete set (a subset of A×B) rather than a vague 'rule'; this removes ambiguity and allows set-theoretic manipulations. (Examples and graphs are given to illustrate.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain, codomain, range
rubrics_metrics.description: For f : A → B, the set A is the domain, B is the codomain, and the range is { f(a) : a ∈ A } = { b : (a,b) ∈ f }.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Range is always a subset of the codomain. The codomain is a matter of choice/context (not intrinsic): any set containing the range can serve as the codomain. Examples illustrate cases where range ≠ codomain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization of functions (graphs vs arrow diagrams)
rubrics_metrics.description: Functions whose domain/codomain are numeric sets are best visualized with conventional graphs; for finite or generic sets, arrow diagrams (draw sets side-by-side and arrows from a to f(a)) are more appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two styles of depiction (subset of A×B grid vs arrows) are shown and guidance given about when each is natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notation for functions on Cartesian-product domains
rubrics_metrics.description: If a function's domain is a Cartesian product (e.g., A×A), it is common to write f(m,n) instead of f((m,n)) for convenience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is essentially a notational convenience; the text notes it is analogous to writing f x instead of f(x).

rubrics_metrics.name: Equality of functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two functions f : A → B and g : C → D are equal if f = g as sets. Equivalently, when domains coincide, f = g iff f(x) = g(x) for every x in the domain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equal functions must have equal domains; they may have different codomains yet be equal (because codomain is not intrinsic). Example: f : Z → N and g : Z → Z defined by same rule can be equal as functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injective (one-to-one) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : A → B is injective if for all a,a' ∈ A, a ≠ a' implies f(a) ≠ f(a').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual description: unequal elements of A map to unequal elements of B. Examples: x^3 on R is injective; x^2 on R is not. To prove injectivity, two main approaches are given (direct and contrapositive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Surjective (onto) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A function f : A → B is surjective if for every b ∈ B there exists a ∈ A with f(a) = b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual description: every element of B has an arrow coming to it from some element of A. Surjectivity depends on the chosen codomain (e.g., x^2 is surjective onto [0,∞) but not onto R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bijective definition
rubrics_metrics.description: A function is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bijective functions are precisely those that are one-to-one correspondences between domain and codomain; bijectivity is tied to invertibility (developed in the inverse-functions section).

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove injectivity (direct and contrapositive methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Direct approach: assume a,a' ∈ A and a ≠ a', then show f(a) ≠ f(a'). Contrapositive approach: assume f(a) = f(a') and deduce a = a'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The contrapositive approach is often easier, especially for functions defined by algebraic formulas, because it starts with an equation f(a)=f(a') and manipulates it to show a=a'.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to disprove injectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a function is not injective, exhibit two distinct elements a ≠ a' in the domain with f(a) = f(a').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A single counterexample suffices; several textbook examples show how unequal inputs map to the same output.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to prove surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f : A → B is surjective, prove ∀ b ∈ B ∃ a ∈ A such that f(a) = b. Practically: take an arbitrary b ∈ B and produce or solve for an a (often by solving f(a)=b).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Finding the appropriate a may require algebraic manipulation or constructive reasoning; providing an explicit formula for a in terms of b suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to disprove surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: To show f is not surjective, show ∃ b ∈ B such that ∀ a ∈ A, f(a) ≠ b.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide a concrete b in the codomain with no preimage in the domain. Examples show choosing an unreachable b (e.g., negative for x^2:R→R).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pigeonhole principle (function version)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A and B are finite sets and f : A → B is any function, then (1) if |A| > |B|, f is not injective; (2) if |A| < |B|, f is not surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This formulation connects counting to injectivity/surjectivity; examples demonstrate nonconstructive existence results (e.g., two subsets with equal sums, two Texans with same hair count). The proof uses cardinality comparisons of domain and codomain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of functions (definition and domain/codomain condition)
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and g : B → C (codomain of f equals domain of g), then g∘f : A → C is defined by g∘f(x) = g(f(x)). Composition also makes sense if range(f) ⊆ domain(g).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with order: g∘f means apply f first, then g. Composition may be undefined if codomain/domain mismatch; examples illustrate both valid and invalid compositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Properties of composition (associativity and non-commutativity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Composition is associative: (h∘g)∘f = h∘(g∘f) when types match. Composition is not commutative in general: g∘f need not equal f∘g.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of associativity is by evaluating both sides at an arbitrary x. Examples show g∘f and f∘g can produce different formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: If f : A → B and g : B → C, then (a) if both f and g are injective, g∘f is injective; (b) if both f and g are surjective, g∘f is surjective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof outlines: for injectivity, g(f(x))=g(f(y)) ⇒ f(x)=f(y) (since g injective) ⇒ x=y (since f injective). For surjectivity, given c∈C pick b with g(b)=c (g surjective) and a with f(a)=b (f surjective), then g(f(a))=c.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity function
rubrics_metrics.description: For a set A, the identity function i_A : A → A is defined by i_A(x) = x for every x ∈ A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: i_A is bijective (trivially injective and surjective). Identity functions act as neutral elements for composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inverse relation (and inverse of a function as relation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given a relation R from A to B, the inverse relation R^{-1} is the relation from B to A defined by R^{-1} = { (y,x) : (x,y) ∈ R }. If f is a bijective function, f^{-1} will be a function from B to A obtained by reversing ordered pairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagrams show R and R^{-1} as arrow diagrams with arrows reversed. Examples illustrate that the inverse of a non-function relation may fail to be a function (multiple arrows may go out of an element in R^{-1}).
